claim: Forty of the 51 B. distachyon accessions tested exhibited a robust SD-vernalization response.
source: Forty of the accessions exhibited a robust SD-vernalization response: these accessions flowered rapidly after the shift from SD to LD, but in LD alone flowering occurred only after quite long periods of growth.
evidence: Based on experimental data from growing 51 accessions under different photoperiod conditions and measuring flowering time.

claim: B. distachyon is an obligate LD plant as meristems remained vegetative after 150 days of growth in SD in all 51 accessions tested.
source: The accessions never flowered when grown solely in SD (Figure 1A and B, Supplementary file 1 and S2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Materials and methods contains the rationale for the controls); furthermore, dissections on the parent culm revealed that the meristems were still vegetative after 150 days of growth in SD in all 51 accessions tested, consistent with our previous studies (Ream et al., 2014; Gordon et al., 2017) indicating that B. distachyon is an obligate LD plant.
evidence: Experimental data from dissections showing vegetative meristems after 150 days in SD, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SD vernalization is a quantitative response where longer periods of SD exposure result in more rapid flowering.
source: Like cold-mediated vernalization, the SD response is quantitative—longer periods of SD exposure result in more rapid flowering in the SD-responsive accessions (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on time course experiments showing flowering time decreases with longer SD exposure.

claim: Eight weeks of SD exposure saturates the SD-vernalization response.
source: Furthermore, 8 weeks of SD exposure saturates the SD-vernalization response.
evidence: Based on time course experimental data showing no additional benefit beyond 8 weeks.

claim: SD vernalization is effective at multiple developmental stages including early and later stages.
source: All of the SD vernalized plants flowered within 35 days after shifting back into LD, with four additional leaves appearing on the parent culm before flowers were visible (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), indicating the SD vernalization is equally effective at early and later developmental stages.
evidence: Experimental data from plants exposed to SD at different developmental stages (0, 2, 4, 6 weeks in LD before SD treatment).

claim: SD responsiveness segregates as a single, dominant locus in mapping populations.
source: In all populations, SD responsiveness segregated as a single, dominant locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) that mapped as a large-effect QTL near the bottom of chromosome 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on genetic mapping data from F2 populations.

claim: A threonine to lysine substitution at position 94 (T94K) in FTL9 is found in all 11 SD non-responsive accessions but not in any of the 40 SD-responsive accessions.
source: However, there is one gene in the interval that is preferentially expressed in SD, and this gene exhibits a one nucleotide change in all 11 SD non-responsive accessions that is not found in any of the 40 SD-responsive accessions; this change results in a threonine to lysine substitution at position 94 (T94K) in an FT paralog (Supplementary file 1–2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2—source data 2) referred to as FT-like 9 (Bradi2g49795; FTL9) (Higgins et al., 2010; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of all 51 accessions and correlation with phenotype.

claim: Reducing FTL9 expression using artificial microRNAs eliminates the SD-vernalization response in SD-responsive accessions.
source: First, reducing FTL9 expression in the SD-responsive accessions Koz3 and Bd21-3 using artificial microRNAs (amiRNAs) eliminates the SD-vernalization response (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic plants with reduced FTL9 expression showing loss of SD vernalization response.

claim: amiRNA knockdown of FTL9 does not affect cold-mediated vernalization.
source: However, the amiRNA lines remain fully responsive to cold-mediated vernalization demonstrating that the role of FTL9 is specific to the SD-vernalization pathway (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Experimental data showing amiRNA lines respond normally to cold vernalization.

claim: Constitutive expression of FTL9 from SD-responsive accessions causes LD-grown transgenic plants to behave as if they were vernalized without prior cold or SD treatment.
source: Second, constitutive expression of an FTL9 cDNA from the SD-responsive accessions Koz3 and Bd21 under the control of the maize ubiquitin promoter in both SD-responsive (Bd21-3 and Koz3) and non-responsive accessions (Bd29-1), which results in FTL9 expression in LD, causes LD-grown transgenic plants to behave as if they were vernalized without prior cold or SD treatment both in terms of accelerated flowering as well as expression of VERNALIZATION1 (VRN1), a MADS box transcription factor related to the APETALA/FRUITFUL family of genes in Arabidopsis thaliana, that is a marker of the vernalized state in grasses (Woods et al., 2014a; Yan et al., 2003; Preston and Kellogg, 2008) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic plants constitutively expressing FTL9 showing early flowering and VRN1 expression, with citations to support VRN1 as a vernalization marker.

claim: Constitutive expression of the FTL9 cDNA from the SD-non-responsive accession Bd1-1 did not affect flowering behavior.
source: In contrast, constitutive expression of the FTL9 cDNA from the SD-non-responsive accession Bd1-1 did not affect the flowering behavior of transgenic lines (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 3) indicating that the T94K change is likely to disrupt FTL9 function consistent with the recessive nature of this allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and that the T94K change occurs in a highly conserved amino acid in this family of proteins in plants and animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic plants expressing the Bd1-1 FTL9 allele showing no phenotypic effect, combined with sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Overexpression of FTL9 does not result in rapid flowering when plants are grown in SD whereas overexpression of FT1 results in rapid flowering in SD.
source: Overexpression of FTL9 does not result in rapid flowering when plants are grown in SD whereas overexpression of FT1 results in rapid flowering in SD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Experimental data comparing flowering phenotypes of FTL9 and FT1 overexpression lines in SD.

claim: The T94K change at FTL9 arose once and was maintained by positive selection throughout outcrossing to diverse accessions.
source: However, a phylogenetic analysis focusing on the 65 kb interval containing FTL9 indicates that in all of the SD-non-responsive accessions the 65 kb FTL9 interval is highly conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B) despite other regions of the genome being divergent. This suggests that the FTL9 variant associated with loss of SD responsiveness arose once and was then maintained by positive selection throughout outcrossing to diverse accessions.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing conservation of the FTL9 interval in all non-responsive accessions despite genome-wide divergence.

claim: FTL9 mRNA is barely detectable in LD, whereas its expression is 350-fold greater in SD.
source: Consistent with its role in SD vernalization, FTL9 mRNA is barely detectable in LD, whereas its expression is 350-fold greater in SD (Figure 3A).
evidence: Gene expression data from qRT-PCR comparing FTL9 levels in SD versus LD.

claim: When SD-grown plants are shifted to LD, FTL9 mRNA levels decline within a few days.
source: When SD-grown plants are shifted to LD, FTL9 mRNA levels decline within a few days (Figure 3A).
evidence: Gene expression data from plants shifted from SD to LD showing decreased FTL9 expression.

claim: FTL9 mRNA levels remain constant over 10 weeks of SD exposure.
source: We tested whether the quantitative aspect of SD vernalization might be correlated with increasing expression of FTL9 during the course of growth in SD, but FTL9 mRNA levels remained the same over 10 weeks of SD exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Gene expression data from a time course experiment in SD.

claim: FTL9 exhibits a diurnal expression pattern in SD with mRNA levels increasing during the night to a peak at dawn and declining during the day to a minimum at dusk.
source: Finally, FTL9 exhibits a diurnal expression pattern in SD with mRNA levels increasing during the night to a peak at dawn and declining during the day to a minimum at dusk.
evidence: Gene expression data from diurnal time course experiments.

claim: In LD there is no detectable diurnal expression difference for FTL9; expression remains low throughout a 20 hr LD.
source: In LD there is no detectable diurnal expression difference; FTL9 expression remains low throughout a 20 hr LD (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Gene expression data from diurnal time course in LD conditions.

claim: When plants are shifted from SD to free-run, constant-dark conditions, FTL9 mRNA levels plummeted and did not oscillate.
source: When plants are shifted from SD to free-run, constant-dark conditions, FTL9 mRNA levels plummeted and did not oscillate, indicating that diurnally oscillating FTL9 expression requires short day/long night cycles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Gene expression data from plants in constant darkness showing loss of FTL9 expression and oscillation.

claim: FTL9 is part of a FT-like gene family that has expanded to 14 members in grasses.
source: FTL9 is part of a FT-like gene family that has expanded to 14 members in grasses (Higgins et al., 2010 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and citation to previous work on FT-like gene family.

claim: FTL10 is the B. distachyon ortholog of barley FT3.
source: FTL10 (Bradi2g19670) is the B. distachyon ortholog of barley FT3 (Higgins et al., 2010; Halliwell et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: FTL10 and FTL9 are closely related paralogs that resulted from a grass-specific duplication event.
source: FTL10 and FTL9 are closely related paralogs that resulted from a grass-specific duplication event, and thus FTL10 and FTL9 reside in sister clades (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis showing grass-specific duplication.

claim: FTL10 expression in B. distachyon is not modulated by day-length and its expression level is quite low in all photoperiod and temperature conditions tested.
source: FT3 is up-regulated in SD in barley (Faure et al., 2007) and wheat (Lv et al., 2014), whereas FTL10 expression in B. distachyon is not modulated by day-length and its expression level is quite low in all photoperiod and temperature conditions tested (Figure 3D).
evidence: Gene expression data from B. distachyon under various conditions, with citations to barley and wheat studies for comparison.

claim: Constitutive expression of FTL10 results in flowering during transgenic line generation in tissue culture and rapid flowering in SD.
source: However, constitutive expression of FTL10 from the maize ubiquitin promoter results in flowering during transgenic line generation in tissue culture (Figure 3E) and rapid flowering in SD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3I,J) similar to the effects of expression of other FT1 orthologs in B. distachyon (Figure 2—figure supplement 3I,J; Ream et al., 2014) and wheat (Lv et al., 2014) indicating that FTL10 has the ability to induce flowering.
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic plants constitutively expressing FTL10, with citations to similar findings in other species.

claim: The FTL9 ortholog in sorghum and maize (CENTRORADIALIS 12; CN12) is expressed only in SD.
source: For example, like FTL9 in B. distachyon, the FTL9 ortholog in sorghum and maize (CENTRORADIALIS 12; CN12) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 6) is also expressed only in SD (Murphy et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2011; Wolabu et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and citations to studies in sorghum and maize.

claim: In sorghum and maize, CN12 and SD expressed CN8 (the FTL10/FT3 ortholog) are both florigenic.
source: However, in sorghum and maize, which are SD-flowering or day neutral plants, CN12 and SD expressed CN8 (the FTL10/FT3 ortholog) are both florigenic similar to FTL10/FT3 (Meng et al., 2011; Lazakis et al., 2011; Wolabu et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on citations to studies in sorghum and maize showing florigen activity.

claim: FTL9 expression is significantly elevated in phyC mutants grown in LD compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, FTL9 expression is significantly elevated in phyC mutants grown in LD compared to wild type across all time points tested (Figure 4A).
evidence: Gene expression data comparing FTL9 levels in phyC mutants versus wild type in LD.

claim: FT1 does not act as a LD repressor of FTL9 in B. distachyon.
source: To determine if FT1 represses FTL9 in B. distachyon, we evaluated FTL9 expression in UBI:FT1 transgenic lines grown in SD, a condition in which BdFT1 is not expressed in wild-type plants. FTL9 expression levels were similar between UBI:FT1 and wild-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H); thus, it is unlikely that FT1 acts as a LD repressor of FTL9 in B. distachyon.
evidence: Gene expression data from FT1 overexpression lines showing no effect on FTL9 expression.

claim: The level of FTL9 expression is inversely correlated with the level of expression of VRN2.
source: VERNALIZATION2 (VRN2) which contains a putative zinc finger and a CONSTANS, CONSTANS-like, and TIMING OF CAB1 domain (Yan et al., 2004) is another candidate gene that might repress FTL9 during LD because VRN2 expression is abolished in the phyC mutant (Woods et al., 2014a) and the level of FTL9 expression is inversely correlated with the level of expression of VRN2 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Gene expression data showing inverse correlation between VRN2 and FTL9, with citations to VRN2 characterization and phyC mutant studies.

claim: VRN2 is a repressor of flowering, and its expression is a function of day-length.
source: VRN2 is a flowering repressor, and its expression is a function of day-length (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Dubcovsky et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2016).
evidence: Gene expression data showing day-length dependent VRN2 expression, with citations to previous studies.

claim: VRN2 controls FTL9 expression in B. distachyon.
source: That VRN2 controls FTL9 expression in B. distachyon is supported by the upregulation of FTL9 in LD when VRN2 expression is suppressed by amiRNAs (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and the lack of FTL9 expression and lack of acquisition of competence to flower in SD when VRN2 is constitutively expressed (Figure 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from VRN2 knockdown and overexpression lines showing effects on FTL9 expression and SD vernalization response.

claim: Over- or under-expression of FTL9 does not affect VRN2 mRNA levels.
source: The regulation is one way: over- or under-expression of FTL9 does not affect VRN2 mRNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Gene expression data from FTL9 transgenic lines showing no effect on VRN2 expression.

claim: Prolonged exposure of Koz3 to SD followed by a shift to LD results in the up-regulation of both FT1 and VRN1.
source: However, prolonged exposure of Koz3 (SD vernalization responsive) to SD followed by a shift to LD (SD-LD) results in the up-regulation of both FT1 and VRN1, whereas this treatment does not result in FT1 and VRN1 expression in the SD non-responsive accession Bd1-1 (Figure 5).
evidence: Gene expression data comparing FT1 and VRN1 levels in SD-responsive versus non-responsive accessions after SD-LD shift.

claim: SD-mediated vernalization is attenuated in amiVRN1 transgenic lines.
source: As previously shown for cold-mediated vernalization (Woods et al., 2016), SD-mediated vernalization is attenuated in amiVRN1 transgenic lines (Figure 5C,D), further corroborating that the cold- and SD-mediated vernalization pathways converge on enabling expression of genes like VRN1 when plants are exposed to inductive LD.
evidence: Experimental data from VRN1 knockdown lines showing reduced SD vernalization response, with citation to cold vernalization study.

claim: The loss of FTL9 activity has no effect on cold-mediated vernalization.
source: It is important to note that the loss of FTL9 activity has no effect on cold-mediated vernalization (Figure 2) demonstrating that there are features that define the two pathways as separate.
evidence: Experimental data showing FTL9 knockdown lines respond normally to cold vernalization.

claim: SD-non-responsive accessions require longer periods of cold exposure than SD-responsive accessions to become fully vernalized.
source: Interestingly, the SD-non-responsive accessions also require a longer period of cold exposure than the SD-responsive accessions to become fully vernalized (Gordon et al., 2017 and Figure 1C; Supplementary file 3) which is consistent with the SD-non-responsive accessions having undergone adaptation for later spring flowering.
evidence: Experimental data on cold vernalization requirements, with citation to previous study.

claim: The non-responsive accessions tend to have been collected at higher latitudes than the responsive accessions.
source: Also, consistent with this model of the adaptive value of loss of FTL9 activity, the non-responsive accessions tend to have been collected at higher latitudes than the responsive accessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2); however, latitude is only one of many factors that may relate to the latest date of a damaging freeze.
evidence: Geographic data on accession collection sites showing latitudinal distribution.

claim: The SD vernalization response is effective when SD-grown accessions are shifted into photoperiods of 12 hr or longer.
source: All three SD-responsive accessions flowered more rapidly after exposure to SD when the day-length was 12 hr or longer (Figure 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from plants shifted from SD to various photoperiods.

claim: In B. distachyon 12 hr is the minimal day-length that is still partially inductive for flowering.
source: In B. distachyon 12 hr is the minimal day-length that is still partially inductive for flowering (Ream et al., 2014; Woods et al., 2017a).
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies characterizing photoperiod requirements.

claim: The flowering effect of SD vernalization is manifest at the same inductive photoperiods as cold-mediated vernalization.
source: Thus, the flowering effect of SD vernalization is manifest at the same inductive photoperiods as cold-mediated vernalization.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing both SD and cold vernalization require similar photoperiods for flowering.

claim: SD vernalization provides competence to flower by enabling the expression of VRN1 and FT1 once plants are in LD.
source: Thus, SD vernalization provides competence to flower by enabling the expression of VRN1 and FT1 once plants are in LD.
evidence: Based on gene expression data showing VRN1 and FT1 upregulation after SD-LD shift in responsive accessions.

claim: FTL9 appears to be grass-specific.
source: The fact that FTL9 appears to be grass-specific but SD-mediated vernalization exists in other groups of plants suggests that SD-mediated vernalization likely evolved independently several times as well.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis showing FTL9 only in grasses and knowledge that SD vernalization occurs in other plant families.

claim: SD-mediated vernalization likely evolved independently several times in flowering plants.
source: The fact that FTL9 appears to be grass-specific but SD-mediated vernalization exists in other groups of plants suggests that SD-mediated vernalization likely evolved independently several times as well.
evidence: Based on the grass-specific nature of FTL9 and the occurrence of SD vernalization in other plant families.

claim: Cold-mediated vernalization likely evolved independently multiple times as flowering plants were radiating some 140 million years ago.
source: Advances in understanding the molecular underpinnings of cold-mediated vernalization in several different plant groups as well as knowledge from paleobotany and earth climate history indicate that cold-mediated vernalization likely evolved independently multiple times as flowering plants were radiating some 140 million years ago (e.g., Bouché et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on citation to previous work on cold vernalization evolution.

claim: The T94K change occurs in a highly conserved amino acid in the FT family of proteins in plants and animals.
source: In contrast, constitutive expression of the FTL9 cDNA from the SD-non-responsive accession Bd1-1 did not affect the flowering behavior of transgenic lines (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 3) indicating that the T94K change is likely to disrupt FTL9 function consistent with the recessive nature of this allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and that the T94K change occurs in a highly conserved amino acid in this family of proteins in plants and animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment showing conservation of the affected amino acid across species.

claim: VRN1 is a MADS box transcription factor related to the APETALA/FRUITFUL family of genes in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Second, constitutive expression of an FTL9 cDNA from the SD-responsive accessions Koz3 and Bd21 under the control of the maize ubiquitin promoter in both SD-responsive (Bd21-3 and Koz3) and non-responsive accessions (Bd29-1), which results in FTL9 expression in LD, causes LD-grown transgenic plants to behave as if they were vernalized without prior cold or SD treatment both in terms of accelerated flowering as well as expression of VERNALIZATION1 (VRN1), a MADS box transcription factor related to the APETALA/FRUITFUL family of genes in Arabidopsis thaliana, that is a marker of the vernalized state in grasses (Woods et al., 2014a; Yan et al., 2003; Preston and Kellogg, 2008) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies characterizing VRN1.

claim: VRN1 is a marker of the vernalized state in grasses.
source: Second, constitutive expression of an FTL9 cDNA from the SD-responsive accessions Koz3 and Bd21 under the control of the maize ubiquitin promoter in both SD-responsive (Bd21-3 and Koz3) and non-responsive accessions (Bd29-1), which results in FTL9 expression in LD, causes LD-grown transgenic plants to behave as if they were vernalized without prior cold or SD treatment both in terms of accelerated flowering as well as expression of VERNALIZATION1 (VRN1), a MADS box transcription factor related to the APETALA/FRUITFUL family of genes in Arabidopsis thaliana, that is a marker of the vernalized state in grasses (Woods et al., 2014a; Yan et al., 2003; Preston and Kellogg, 2008) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies establishing VRN1 as a vernalization marker.

claim: PHYTOCHROME C (PHYC) is a red light receptor.
source: PHYTOCHROME C (PHYC) is a red light receptor and in phyC mutants the LD photoperiod flowering pathway is abolished and mutant plants are extremely delayed in flowering and have the appearance of SD-grown plants when grown under LD (Woods et al., 2014a).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study characterizing PHYC.

claim: In phyC mutants the LD photoperiod flowering pathway is abolished and mutant plants are extremely delayed in flowering.
source: PHYTOCHROME C (PHYC) is a red light receptor and in phyC mutants the LD photoperiod flowering pathway is abolished and mutant plants are extremely delayed in flowering and have the appearance of SD-grown plants when grown under LD (Woods et al., 2014a).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study characterizing phyC mutant phenotype.

claim: VRN2 expression is abolished in the phyC mutant.
source: VERNALIZATION2 (VRN2) which contains a putative zinc finger and a CONSTANS, CONSTANS-like, and TIMING OF CAB1 domain (Yan et al., 2004) is another candidate gene that might repress FTL9 during LD because VRN2 expression is abolished in the phyC mutant (Woods et al., 2014a) and the level of FTL9 expression is inversely correlated with the level of expression of VRN2 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study showing VRN2 expression in phyC mutant.

claim: VRN2 contains a putative zinc finger and a CONSTANS, CONSTANS-like, and TIMING OF CAB1 domain.
source: VERNALIZATION2 (VRN2) which contains a putative zinc finger and a CONSTANS, CONSTANS-like, and TIMING OF CAB1 domain (Yan et al., 2004) is another candidate gene that might repress FTL9 during LD because VRN2 expression is abolished in the phyC mutant (Woods et al., 2014a) and the level of FTL9 expression is inversely correlated with the level of expression of VRN2 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study characterizing VRN2 protein structure.

claim: In wheat, VRN2 is down-regulated by both cold and short days.
source: This expression pattern contrasts with that of VRN2 in a SD-vernalization responsive variety of wheat in which VRN2 levels remain at low SD levels after a shift to LD (Dubcovsky et al., 2006). In wheat, VRN2 is down-regulated by both cold and short days suggesting that this gene might play a role in the integration of the SD vernalization and vernalization pathways (Dubcovsky et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on citation to study of VRN2 in wheat.

claim: VRN2 is up-regulated during cold in B. distachyon.
source: This is unlikely to be the case in B. distachyon as VRN2 is up-regulated during the cold (Ream et al., 2014) and VRN2 down-regulation in SD is not maintained during a SD-LD shift (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study and gene expression data from SD-LD shift experiment.

claim: In rice, expression of the VRN2 ortholog GHd7 is reduced in SD enabling expression of Hd3 which encodes a florigen.
source: For example, in rice, in which SD are inductive for flowering, expression of the VRN2 ortholog GHd7 (Woods et al., 2016) is reduced in SD enabling expression of Hd3 which encodes a florigen (Xue et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on citations to studies in rice.

claim: In wheat and barley, the florigen FT3 is expressed in SD, and this SD-specific expression of FT3 is correlated with lower levels of VRN2 expression in SD.
source: Also, in wheat and barley, the florigen FT3 is expressed in SD, and this SD-specific expression of FT3 is correlated with lower levels of VRN2 expression in SD (Dubcovsky et al., 2006; Kikuchi et al., 2009; Casao et al., 2011b).
evidence: Based on citations to studies in wheat and barley.

claim: In barley varieties with loss of function mutations in VRN2, FT3 expression is elevated under LD conditions.
source: Furthermore, in barley varieties with loss of function mutations in VRN2 results in elevated FT3 expression under LD conditions that do not typically induce its expression (Casao et al., 2011b).
evidence: Based on citation to study in barley.

claim: Repression of VRN1 before cold-mediated vernalization is associated with high levels of H3K27me3 at VRN1 chromatin in both barley and B. distachyon.
source: For example, repression of VRN1 before cold-mediated vernalization is associated with high levels of H3K27me3 at VRN1 chromatin in both barley and B. distachyon (Oliver et al., 2009; Lomax et al., 2018; Woods et al., 2017b).
evidence: Based on citations to studies on VRN1 chromatin modifications.

claim: A candidate gene underlying a QTL that confers the ability of certain wheat and barley varieties to flower in SD (Ppd-H2) is a paralog of FT referred to as FT3.
source: Studies in wheat and barley indicate that a candidate gene underlying a QTL that confers the ability of certain varieties to flower in SD (Ppd-H2) (Laurie et al., 1995) is a paralog of FT referred to as FT3 (Faure et al., 2007; Kikuchi et al., 2009; Casao et al., 2011a).
evidence: Based on citations to studies in wheat and barley identifying FT3.

claim: The dominant FT3 allele, which enables SD flowering, is often found in spring barley cultivars grown in more southern latitudes.
source: The dominant FT3 allele, which enables SD flowering, is often found in spring barley cultivars grown in more southern latitudes, whereas the recessive allele is typically associated with winter cultivars grown in more northern latitudes (Casao et al., 2011a).
evidence: Based on citation to study on FT3 allele distribution in barley.

claim: FT3 is implicated in actual flowering in SD in barley as opposed to the competence to flower in LD that is conferred by SD-specific expression of FTL9 in B. distachyon.
source: FT3 is implicated in actual flowering in SD in barley as opposed to the competence to flower in LD that is conferred by SD-specific expression of FTL9 in B. distachyon.
evidence: Based on comparison of functional data from barley and B. distachyon studies.

claim: In barley cultivars that can flower in SD, HvFT1 has been postulated to be a repressor of HvFT3.
source: One candidate gene is FT1; in barley cultivars that can flower in SD, HvFT1 has been postulated to be a repressor of HvFT3—the SD-expressed paralog of FTL9 discussed above (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) —because relatively high HvFT3 expression in SD precedes the expression of HvFT1 and, as HvFT1 expression levels increase in SD, HvFT3 expression decreases (Kikuchi et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on citation to study in barley showing expression correlation.

claim: There are barley varieties that do not flower in SD because their FT3 alleles have lesions in the coding region.
source: There are other barley varieties that do not flower in SD because their FT3 alleles have lesions in the coding region (Kikuchi et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on citation to study identifying FT3 lesions in barley.

claim: All accessions of B. distachyon analyzed are obligate LD plants because the florigenic member of the clade, FTL10, is not expressed at sufficient levels to cause flowering in SD.
source: All accessions of B. distachyon that we have analyzed are obligate LD plants because the florigenic member of the clade, FTL10, is not expressed at sufficient levels to cause flowering in SD and the other member of the clade, FTL9, evolved the different function of providing competence to flower rather than directly promoting flowering like it does in sorghum and maize.
evidence: Based on gene expression data and functional analysis of FTL10 and FTL9.

claim: FTL9 evolved the function of providing competence to flower rather than directly promoting flowering like it does in sorghum and maize.
source: All accessions of B. distachyon that we have analyzed are obligate LD plants because the florigenic member of the clade, FTL10, is not expressed at sufficient levels to cause flowering in SD and the other member of the clade, FTL9, evolved the different function of providing competence to flower rather than directly promoting flowering like it does in sorghum and maize.
evidence: Based on functional analysis comparing FTL9 in B. distachyon to orthologs in sorghum and maize.

claim: SD-mediated vernalization was first described in rye in 1937.
source: SD-mediated vernalization was first described in rye in 1937 (Purvis and Gregory, 1937) and has been described in wheat and barley (Evans, 1987; Heide, 1994; Dubcovsky et al., 2006); however, sequence data available to date have not revealed a clear ortholog of FTL9 in wheat or barley (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Faure et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on citations to historical and recent studies, and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Sequence data available to date have not revealed a clear ortholog of FTL9 in wheat or barley.
source: SD-mediated vernalization was first described in rye in 1937 (Purvis and Gregory, 1937) and has been described in wheat and barley (Evans, 1987; Heide, 1994; Dubcovsky et al., 2006); however, sequence data available to date have not revealed a clear ortholog of FTL9 in wheat or barley (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Faure et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and citation to previous sequence studies.

claim: In beet, an FT family member is an inhibitor of flowering that is key to establishing a requirement for vernalization.
source: In beet, an FT family member is an inhibitor of flowering that is key to establishing a requirement for vernalization (Pin et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on citation to study in beet.

claim: The work in B. distachyon reveals a new role for an FT family member: the establishment of competence to flower without direct florigen activity.
source: Our work in B. distachyon reveals a new role for an FT family member: the establishment of competence to flower without direct florigen activity.
evidence: Based on the functional characterization of FTL9 showing it confers competence but does not directly induce flowering.

claim: The adaptive value of an active FTL9 and a SD-vernalization response may be to ensure that vernalization occurs in mild climates in which SD may be a more reliable indicator of winter than cold.
source: The adaptive value of an active FTL9 and a SD-vernalization response, which is the ancestral state, may be to ensure that vernalization occurs in mild climates in which SD may be a more reliable indicator of winter than cold.
evidence: Based on speculation about adaptive significance given the distribution and function of FTL9.

claim: The adaptive value of loss of FTL9 activity might be to enable B. distachyon to grow in regions with a more variable spring climate in which a robust SD-vernalization response might lead to flowering before the danger of a hard freeze had passed.
source: The adaptive value of loss of FTL9 activity and the corresponding loss of the SD-vernalization response might be to enable B. distachyon to grow in regions with a more variable spring climate in which a robust SD-vernalization response might lead to flowering before the danger of a hard freeze, which would damage sensitive floral organs, had passed.
evidence: Based on speculation about adaptive significance given the distribution and phenotype of non-responsive accessions.

claim: The loss of a vernalization requirement in Arabidopsis thaliana arose independently many times due to loss-of-function mutations in FRIGIDA.
source: That a lesion in FTL9 that appears to have undergone positive selection arose once is in contrast to the loss of a vernalization requirement in Arabidopsis thaliana which arose independently many times due to loss-of-function mutations in FRIGIDA (Le Corre et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on citation to study on FRIGIDA in Arabidopsis.

claim: The SD-vernalization response exists in an array of species spanning flowering plant diversification.
source: Similar to cold-mediated vernalization, the SD-mediated vernalization response is found in an array of species spanning flowering plant diversification (Chouard, 1960; Heide, 1994).
evidence: Based on citations to studies documenting SD vernalization in diverse species.
